statement.p: Let \vec F = 5 y\vec i + 6 x\vec j, \phi = \frac{8}{3} x^3 + 5 x y, and h = y - 4 x^2.
How are \vec F - \nabla \phi and \nabla h related?

p.em: (Note that this shows that \vec F - \nabla \phi is parallel to \nabla h.)

statement.p: (b) Use \phi and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for Line Integrals to evaluate \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r, where C is the oriented path on a contour of h from P(0,8) to Q(5,108).

static.solution:
(a) We have 
abla\phi = \langle (8 x^2 + 5 y)\vec i + 5 y\vec j and so \vec F - 
abla\phi = -8x^{2}\,\mathit{\vec i}+x\,\mathit{\vec j}. Then 
abla h = -8x\,\mathit{\vec i}+\,\mathit{\vec j}, so \vec F - 
abla\phi = x
abla h, and \vec F - 
abla \phi is a multiple of 
abla h and so is parallel to it.
(b) By part (a) the vector fields \vec F and 
abla \phi have the same components perpendicular to 
abla h, which is to say the same components in the direction of the level curve C of h. Thus, the line integrals of \vec F and 
abla \phi along C are equal. Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for Line Integrals, we have \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_C 
abla \phi \cdot d\vec r = \phi(Q)-\phi(P) = 3033.33 - 0 = 3033.33.
